opus-5.5.text:
Well, the big world hypothesis is the idea that the world is vastly larger and more complex than any agent that lives in it. The agent is small, the world is big. And if you take that seriously, then it follows almost immediately that you can't learn everything you need ahead of time. There's just too much. The particular things that matter to you, the particular people you work with, the particular quirks of your job, the way things are changing this week, none of that can be anticipated and baked in during some training phase before you're deployed.

The large language model picture is essentially the opposite assumption. It says, let's gather up as much as we can, train on it all, and then freeze it and send it out into the world. And the hope is that it has learned enough general stuff that it will cope. But in a big world, what you need to know is mostly the specific stuff, the stuff about your situation, and that's precisely what you can't get in advance. You have to learn it on the job, from your own experience, as you go.

So I think the big world hypothesis says that continual learning isn't a nice add-on. It's essential. An agent has to be learning all the time, from its own stream of experience: what it did, what happened, what reward it got. Think about how people work. A new employee isn't valuable on day one because they've memorized everything. They become valuable because over weeks and months they pick up the context, the tacit knowledge, all the particulars. Our current systems mostly don't do that. They try to stuff the particulars into the context window, which is a kind of patch, but it isn't really learning.

And there's a deeper point. In a big world, the agent can't have a correct model of the world. It's always approximating. That means the right thing is not to get the approximation perfect once, but to keep adjusting it, keep tracking a world that's too big to capture. Tracking rather than converging. I think that's where the field needs to go, and I don't think you get there by making the pre-training bigger.

r001.rationale: It says a new employee becomes valuable over time by picking up the context, tacit knowledge, and particulars of the job.

r002.rationale: It explains that the world is too large and changing for an agent to learn everything it needs before deployment.

r003.rationale: It mentions particular people the agent works with, but does not distinguish their preferences from average human preferences.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the big world hypothesis is really the heart of the matter. The idea is that the world is much bigger than the agent. There's vastly more going on than any agent could ever hold in its head, no matter how many parameters it has, no matter how much data it was trained on. The agent is always small relative to the world it has to act in.

And if you take that seriously, then the notion that you could learn everything you need ahead of time, during a training phase, and then be deployed as a finished product, that just doesn't hold up. Because the world you're deployed into is not the world you were trained on. It's going to present you with situations that weren't in the data, that couldn't have been in the data, because they're specific to this moment, this user, this particular configuration of circumstances. The world keeps generating novelty faster than you can anticipate it.

So the right response to a big world is not to try to know everything in advance. It's to be able to learn continually, during the interaction, while you're acting. That's what animals do. That's what people do. We don't finish learning and then go live our lives. We're learning the whole time, and the learning is driven by what actually happens to us, by the consequences of our actions, by experience.

The large language models, as they're currently built, don't do that. They have this enormous frozen store of knowledge from text, and then at deployment the learning essentially stops, or at best it's some shallow thing in the context window. And they're learning from what people have said, not from what happens. That's a crucial difference. Text tells you what people believe about the world. Experience tells you what the world actually does when you push on it. In a big world, the second kind of knowledge is the kind that can't be pre-loaded, because there's always more of it than you could ever have collected.

So I'd say the big world hypothesis is almost an argument against the whole paradigm. It says the important part of intelligence is the part that happens after deployment, not before. And that's the part we've barely begun to build.

r001.rationale: The response discusses continual learning from experience generally, but does not identify learning about one’s particular work environment as a source of human usefulness on the job.

r002.rationale: It says the world keeps generating novel situations that could not have been in training data, so an agent cannot learn everything it needs before deployment.

r003.rationale: The response does not distinguish average human preferences from the preferences of the particular people an agent works with.

astra-6.text:
Well, the big world hypothesis is that the world is much bigger than the agent. There’s always more detail, more things going on, than the agent can represent or learn about. So the idea that you could finish learning and then deploy—that you could have everything you need already in your head—is really at odds with that view.

You can learn a great deal beforehand, of course. But once you’re deployed, you encounter particular circumstances that you couldn’t have anticipated. You have to learn which distinctions matter, what consequences your actions have, and how things are changing. Learning is part of the agent’s ongoing interaction with the world, rather than a preliminary stage that you eventually complete.

And I would distinguish that from merely having a fixed system that can respond to many different inputs. That’s useful, but we want an agent whose experience continually improves how it behaves. In a big world, that job is never finished.

r001.rationale: The response says an agent encounters particular circumstances after deployment, but does not identify learning about one’s work environment as a source of human usefulness on the job.

r002.rationale: It says the world contains more detail than an agent can represent or learn, so deployed circumstances cannot all be anticipated beforehand and learning must continue.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss average human preferences or distinguish them from the preferences of particular people an agent works with.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the big world hypothesis says that the world is much bigger than the agent. There’s always more detail, more complexity, than the agent can represent or learn about. So you shouldn’t imagine that learning is a phase you finish, and then you go out into the world and simply apply what you’ve learned.

You can learn a great deal before deployment. But once you’re deployed, you encounter particular circumstances that you didn’t anticipate, and things change. You have to keep learning. And you have to decide what’s worth learning, because you can’t learn everything.

So the question is less whether a language model has acquired all the knowledge it needs, and more whether it has acquired the ability to adapt through its ongoing interaction with the world. If its parameters are fixed and it’s just producing answers, then an important part of intelligence is missing. We want agents for which learning is a continuing part of their lives.

r001.rationale: The response discusses ongoing learning after deployment but does not identify learning a particular work environment as a source of human usefulness on the job.

r002.rationale: It says the world exceeds what an agent can represent or learn, and that deployed agents encounter unanticipated circumstances, so they cannot finish anticipating all learning needs beforehand.

r003.rationale: The response does not distinguish average human preferences from the preferences of particular people an agent works with.
